summary:
Huancavelica stands under Peru's national framework. The region has no recorded trans-specific law, ordinance, enforcement pattern or incident of its own, so what a trans visitor faces here is the national position as it applies in this department.

At national level, the congressional Plenary approved on 2 April 2025 a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', with narrow listed exceptions. The IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025 argues this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The bill had earlier cleared the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously on 20 February 2025, merging bills 6506 and 8457 introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, with exceptions for custody, required medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage; the trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and noting there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

Violence against trans people is documented at national level. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, covered by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023 (12 trans women) from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denuncias in 2020. The report also recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. These are national figures; no Huancavelica-specific count is available, and raw national totals are not adjusted for population.
tangentialFactors:
The restroom restriction's practical effect in Huancavelica would be mediated by security staff discretion, as Camacho warned, since enforcement of 'biological sex' matching falls to whoever checks documents at a facility. Huancavelica is a predominantly rural, highland department where public facilities of the kind covered by the national statute may be fewer than in Lima, but transit through regional hubs and health facilities still engages the rule.

The national hate-violence data are raw counts across Peru's regions without a per-capita denominator, and no breakdown by department is available; Huancavelica's share of the recorded 54 killings and 170 violation cases over 2020-2023 is not stated in the sources.
localsOnly:
Residents of Huancavelica are subject to the same national statutes as visitors: the article 5 restroom restriction, the absence of a Huancavelica-specific anti-discrimination ordinance, and the national pattern of recorded anti-trans violence. No departmental ordinance, regional government measure, or Huancavelica enforcement incident covering trans people is recorded in the sources.

The IDEHPUCP constitutional challenge and the legislative process on bills 6506 and 8457 are national proceedings in Lima; residents seeking to contest the restriction would engage those same national institutions.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Huancavelica-specific signal was identified in the source inventory: no regional law, ordinance, enforcement pattern, facility incident, or hate-crime case tied to this department appears in any source. The claims above are national-layer findings carried here because the region has nothing of its own to report.

The sources do not resolve whether article 5 of the 2 April 2025 bill was enacted as law or remained a bill at the time of writing, nor whether the 20 February 2025 committee approval and the 2 April 2025 plenary approval refer to the same instrument; the inventory describes both a bill at committee stage in February and plenary approval in April. Whether any Huancavelica public facility has applied an ID check under the new rule is not sourced.
